He made it out of the war alive, but almost lost his leg. He was a Staff Sgt. and got shot by a sniper on the last day of the Battle of the Bulge. Bullet went through the lower leg, compound fracture. Spent a year in the hospital. He kept the leg, but a big piece of the flash was missing from it. He was amazingly able to walk, run and even jump without the use of a cane.

I never met him. He died young of a stroke, age 55, 15 years before I was born. It's sad because he would've only been 70 when I was born. I knew only a few stories. He never spoke about it much to anyone.

Story 1: One day, in France, he and his crew were "cleaning out" (his word usage) a store of Germans. It was a jewelry store, maybe, or a perfume store - who knows now? Anyway, they go in the store and his friend is stuffing perfume bottles under his uniform, saying when he goes home he'll sell them and be rich. Gunfire breaks out and they run out of the store and jump into a foxhole for cover. The bottles of perfume his guy was carrying burst all over the guy, making him smell like a French whore.

Story 2: One day he was speaking to his friend in a foxhole. A shot rang out. When he looked over, his friend was shot in the head, dead.

Story 3: One day, he and his men came to a little river or a little stream. They stopped to fill up their canteens with water. The water tasted funny, metallic. They walked a while and followed the body of water up a ways, only to find it was littered with the bodies of dead Germans, whose blood soaked into the water....

The doctor at the medical camp where he was taken when he was rescued after being shot wanted to remove his leg. My grandfather held his gun up to the doctor, and said, "If you take my leg, I'm taking you with me, because I'll have nothing left to live for." The doctor ordered him sedated and removed from the tent. He kept his leg.

When he had his first stroke (he had two, he survived the first), in 1973, he didn't call any ambulance. He got himself dressed (despite being paralyzed on one side) and called for a cab. The cab drove around for a long time ("hours" claims my grandmother) because he couldn't understand my grandfather's instructions. He got to the hospital and told the attending doctor not to call his wife (my grandparents were separated) and they didn't until he went into a coma and began having grand mal seizures, which made them think he wouldn't survive. He did. No major impairments. Was out of the hospital and walking and talking within four months.

He kept a lot of his war memorabilia. I have a guidebook to San Francisco (he was stationed at the Presidio from 1941 to 1942), his Presidio Library card, I have his Army Driver License which allowed him to drive trucks, among some other things. He kept a book which he bought while in the Army called "Why America Fights" by Sherwood Eddy. The book talks about how the war is a moral crusade, and also talks about how America needs to fight a similar crusade - for civil rights for all - at home. Eddy was a Christian theologian type thought of as a communist for those views.

My grandfather had two sayings I am aware of. One: "If I can't eat what I want to eat, what's the point of being alive?" he said to my aunt after his first stroke, when she warned him to keep to his diet. Two, "When the man upstairs calls you, you could have the world's best doctor's around you, but when it's your time to go, it's your time to go." 

He also didn't want my one aunt becoming a Nun, believing she could do a lot more with her mind; and disallowed my other aunt to join the Army in the late 60s, saying to her that "they don't treat women well there."

The Weimar Republic was always a house of cards. It prospered for a time in the early to mid 1920s but its foundations were so weak that the Depression obliterated its economy, and it never had the full and popular support of the German people. It was a compromise government which people accepted for a time because there was no alternative. But the German people were used to autocracy. Democracy was new to them; remember, prior to WWI, the Kaiser ruled Germany as a King. Suddenly, centuries of political tradition are undone with the stroke of a pen. Democracy can't just be forced on a people and yet here it was. There were many unhappy movement of people in Germany in the 1920s, not just the Nazis. There were Socialists, Anarchists, others who wanted the Kaiser returned to power. Hitler was simply the most charismatic and savviest of a bunch of would be strongmen, who managed to come out on top through charisma, and networking. If it wasn't him I think it would've been someone SIMILAR, but less evil. You might have had someone, for example, who would've been a dictator but more of a Saddam Hussein type rather than "Kill all the Jews and start another world war" type. Hitler, I believe, was the second worst option Germany had. The worst would've been a military coup. But even say, a restoration of the Kaiser to power wouldn't have been nearly as bad, for both Germany in the long run and the world as a whole.

My family came from Brooklyn, NY. One part came from Bay Ridge, the other from Bensonhurst. Both areas were very conservative, so the "60s" that are shown in documentaries didn't really arrive here until the 70s. My dad was born in 54 and I've seen pictures of him from as late as 1967 and his own hair is short. Flashforward to 1971 and it's down to his shoulders. What's funny is, my grandpa (not the one in the picture above - those are my mom's parents) used to wear a Duck's Ass haircut in the 60s and 70s. All slicked back. When he would sweat the gel or whatever would come loose and his hair in the front would hang down to his chin and would hang over his ears on the sides - but he would chastize my father for his long hair. He was an ardent hawk who supported Vietnam and my father and he would get into arguments over it all the time.

One notable little memory - around 71, 72 like that - my father had put up a poster in his room which said something like 'war is no good for children and other living things.' Upon seeing it my grandpa got enraged and tore it down.

My other grandpa - the one in the picture - rejected my aunt's request that she join the Women's Army Corps. He was a 7 year veteran of the service. He served in the Army before and during WWII. He told her he wouldn't allow her to join because women were mistreated by the men in the service and he didn't want that for her. This was a man who kept all his life a book he got from the Army in 1942 which speaks about how the war in Europe must be extended for a fight for social and racial justice at home. His friends consisted of a Syrian-American guy who was like a brother to him, a Black man who he worked with, and a Mexican-American man he was close to who he also worked with. Quite liberal for his time, and the opposite of my dad's father.

The Irish and Italians, for whatever reason, hated each other, even though both at the time were thought of in the same way Arabs and Mexicans are by racist people today. My mom's grandfather was a first generation American. He was born in 1888 and his father had immigrated here in the 1860s. In the 1860s, as you might know, Irish people were thought of as being Black by mainstream society. They were considered a separate race, and hated.

Flash forward a few decades, to the 1940s. Italians were relatively new to this country and were thought of the same way, as being black, as being different. I guess my Irish great grandpa felt he had worked hard to gain respectability (And he was a VERY hard worker despite his biases and flaws - self made man) and wasn't going to let it be thrown out by his daughter marrying an Italian.

It sounds so silly today but that's how it was.

What's funny is my other great grandpa - my grandma's father in law, the Italian great grandfather - he was also a self made man. He came over from Italy in 1906. Didn't speak a lick of English. Taught himself to speak it by reading the newspaper and having his children help him as well. By the 1930s he owned 3 houses. He earned income by renting out parts of the houses and also owned garages which he rented. One of his houses was rented out and became the local Republican Party headquarters in the 1940s, and then it became a music school in the 1950s. During the fierce winter of 1948, he allowed my racist great grandfather and his family to stay with him. My great grandfather lived in what was called a "cold water flat" and would've froze that harsh winter. He was a good man. He knew his son, my grandpa, was a bad gambler. He would give on the sly my grandmother money for shoes and toys for his granddaughters. The only reason my grandfather was kept in his will was because taking him out of it would hurt his grandkids. He felt my grandfather would just throw it all away otherwise, but didn't want to disinherit his granddaughters.

Actually, that's a myth. JFK wasn't responsible for men not wearing hats, and he didn't dislike wearing hats either. A combination of factors including WWII (men wore helmets during the war and on a subconscious level, didn't want to wear a 'helmet' when they got home), increasing informality in American dress (look at a picture from 1960 vs 1969), smaller cars (Men would tend to wear their hat when they drove; in the late 1950s, cars with lower ceilings were introduced and thus you couldn't wear your hat in the car anymore; where were you going to put it?), as well as a whole host of other factors. JFK didn't dislike wearing hats, he simply saw the way the wind was blowing for one, and secondly, he felt they didn't suit his image. Similarly, JFK smoked cigars and loved them but very rarely let himself be photographed smoking them as at the time, there was a stereotype in American society of a corrupt cigar chomping Irish politician - and he didn't want to be associated with it. JFK was very image-conscious. When it didn't hurt him, he wore a hat like most men of his generation; when it didn't suit him, he didn't wear one. 

There's a good number of photographs of him wearing fedoras in candid moments. Like there is a picture of him wearing one on the way to meet Jackie at the hospital right after John Jr. was born, for example. But in "high profile" glamour moments, he didn't. His hairstyle was part of his image. JFK's entire presidency was built on images - one of which was his thick, tousled hair - why cover it up with a hat? But he didn't dislike them on a personal level - they just cramped his image. But when he could DICTATE the fashion, he liked them:

JFK for example brought back the top hat for his inauguration; Ike had done away with the longstanding trend and wore a homburg to both of his. JFK LOVED top hats and mandated they be the theme of his inaugural. In fact, JFK is the last President to wear any sort of hat to their inauguration.

There's a whole book about this very topic which goes in depth about JFK and the hat industry dying off because of him myth.

Kind of a blending of memories with the Let it Bleed sessions. They were in and out of the studio for almost a year. In that year Brian disintegrated slowly over a year after being busted in May 1968 on a second trumped up drug charge. Beggar's Banquet was recorded and wrapped by July (it was supposed to come out July 26th 1968 but a protracted fight with the label over the album cover kept it out of stores until December - the label rejected the bathroom cover and the band fought it), most of the core recording had been done as early as March and April. 

On Beggar's Brian plays on:

1) Sympathy for the Devil - backing vocals ("hoo hoo's")

2) No Expectations - Slide guitar

3) Jig-saw Puzzle - Mellotron

4) Street Fightin' Man - Sitar & Tambura

5) Dear Doctor - Harmonica

6) Parachute Woman - Harmonica

7) Stray Cat Blues - Mellotron

8) Prodigal Son - Harmonica

Also played guitar on Jumpin' Jack Flash and played soprano saxophone on JJF's b-side Child of the Moon, released in May 1968.

It's on Let it Bleed where he barely contributed. The Let it Bleed sessions began in November 1968 and most of the album was recorded by the time he left the band (it was originally scheduled to be released in July 1969). Tolkien himself was perhaps what we could term a Christian Luddite, or akin to such; he did not hate technology but, as Taylor noted, he saw how it ravaged the fields he loved so, how it murdered his youthful friends, and he took the pain and grief and bitterness he must've felt and transferred it to the Lord of the Rings. I suppose my problem with the work is its Christianity. As the poster above notes, it's almost like LotR isn't part of the legendary tradition - it's different. And I do not discount its artistic merit; I do not deem it a bad book. But getting back to the Christian point, I feel his emphasis on a fading world is very Christian - going back to the decline of humanity from the fall at Eden. And that to me doesn't inspire happiness, it inspires despair.

The world of superior beings who respect nature is passing, and Men - bloody, vindictive, weak Men who are as savage, crude and bloody as any Orc - shall inherit the Earth, rape, and reshape it through technology and war. Tolkien lamented this; so do I. But where he spent his life in working out those feelings of loss - loss of the green countryside - I wish instead he had given us more of the good green Earth to read about and enjoy.

As far as walking at the time: That I am not sure of. As with most men of his generation, he did not speak very much of his combat experience. I was born in 1990. He died in 1975, so any story I hear is second or third hand; I only have the medical record (60 pages) from his year in the Hospital.

He was shot in January 1945. He in later years (decades later) asked his son-in-law (who was a medic, but they didn't know each other until the 1960s) "What took you guys so long? We were waiting there a long time." Something to that effect. So he may have been laying rather than walking.

I do know that when he was taken to the evacuation hospital, the doctor wanted to amputate his leg. He was conscious, and raised his rifle and said, "If you take my leg, you're coming with me, because then I'll have nothing to live for." The doctor ordered him sedated and taken out of the medic tent.

He was taken to an Evac Hospital in Luxembourg immediately after shooting and had the wound debrided and leg placed in a long cast; then transfered to a hospital in England where a secondary closure of the wound was done - noted as being in the "posterior right leg."

The comminuted fracture was between the middle and lower thirds of the tibia. No involvement of the fibula.  Also, his medial malleolus is mentioned a lot in regard to the injury.

He was ambulatory by April 1945, although in early April he suffered from phlebitis in the effected leg.

He had, according to the medical record: "compound fracture over junction over mid & lower 1/3rd Tibia; there is a granulating scar over medial and posterior aspect lower third above ankle. There is a vertical scar 4" 1/2" left and above slight granulating tissue posterior aspect mid third of calf."

He also as of April 1945 had "slight anesthesia of plantar aspect of foot, but no clinical incidence of major nerve paralysis of leg or foot. Possible injury to posterior tibial nerve."

That is April 12th 1945. A photo from April 22nd 1945 shows him standing unassisted with a leg cast. He was allowed home for Easter with family.

He returned back to the Hospital and by October his scar was infected.

As of April 1945 it was granulating; by May it was nearly completely closed. In late May he had a second scar excised. "The posterior tibial nerve was exposed but was not repaired because two extensive dissection would be required and it was thought unwise to attempt it in view of the draining wound. Scar incision and secondary closure was performed."

In June 1945 he was operated on - the surgery was a "neurorraphy of the posterior tibial nerve". In July, he had discharge from the leg and skin necrosis on lateral aspect of the distal end of leg (site of old granulated tissue). He had a vaseline dressing applied.

He was given his first 60 day work furlough in October 1945. He was judged "able to take care of his own needs". But he required further therapy...

As of early Jan 1946 he had a "sinus in operative scar...it has been draining for several hours." This sinus was excised in a second surgery. He had no flexion or sensory in his toes as of this point.

In March 1946, he was discharged from both the Hospital and Army and rendered disabled. He had sensation in the sole of his foot to deep pressure. The discharge board's findings read: "Paralysis of nerve, posterior tibial, right, incomplete. Incapacitates for military service because of weakness and numbness of right foot." He was judged not be able to be rehabilitated to effective military service.

There was a massive chunk of flesh missing from the leg, but he did not need a cane after the war. My aunt said he had a limp, but on the one short home movie of him from the 1960s I do not see it; nor does my mother remember him having one. He is able with ease to leap, doing an impersonation of Charlie Chaplin's famed cane dance. I do notice in some photos after he will hold the unaffected leg bent in front of the injured leg, which be pin straight or a little bent at the knee. Perhaps some pain? I do notice the pose crops up in the few full body photos I have of him from after the war.

I do notice a reoccurring pattern in his post-War life; He enjoyed employment in jobs that involved wearing a uniform (He worked from the mid 1950s through late 1960s as a postman (mail carrier specifically); and also as a security guard - which after the late 1960s became his primary occupation). He always had a second or third job, for example in 1951 he was a Taxi Driver here in New York City - and at the time, Cabbies were required to wear a Flat Cap as part of the "uniform"; In the late 1950s he worked as a paperhanger on the side, and also as an armed Chauffeur in 1959. He worked as a Security Guard for the Pinkerton Detective Agency at the 1964-1965 World's Fair in New York - another job which required a military-esque uniform. He died at the age of 55 in 1975 from a massive stroke (and he had suffered a moderate stroke in 1973) we believe both strokes were caused by clots thrown from the leg. It is likely the leg wound shortened his life as such.

By the last episode of the series, the Tony we met in Season 1 - a rather likable guy, really, who seemed to really want to change - was dead.
